result:
Picture your makerspace's front desk, with one odd rule: the person at the desk is locked in a windowless room. They can't see the booking calendar, and they can't open the manuals. They can only read notes slipped under the door and write notes back.

A student slides a note under the door: "Is the laser cutter free Thursday at 3?"

The desk person can't check, so they write a slip: **"Runner, please look up the laser cutter on Thursday at 3."** They slide it out. The runner goes to the calendar, reads it, and slides back a note: **"Booked 2–4pm."** Now the desk person writes the reply to the student: "Thursday at 3 is taken. Want 4:30 instead?" If they wanted to book 4:30, they'd send another slip, and the runner would do that too.

The mapping:
- **The desk person is the model.** It only reads text and writes text.
- **The slip is the tool call.** It is a request that names the errand and gives the details. Writing it does nothing by itself.
- **The runner is your program.** The runner does the real errand, and the model never does.
- **The note that comes back is the tool result.** It's just more text, and the model reads it before deciding what to write next.
- **The loop** is that cycle repeating until the desk person writes an answer instead of another slip.

A common mix-up is thinking the model "uses" the calendar directly. It never touches it. It only decides which slip to write, and the quality of that decision depends on the tool descriptions you give it, like a menu of errands the runner can do. That's why writing clear tool descriptions is one of your mission goals.

The analogy breaks in one place. A real desk person remembers earlier notes. The model starts fresh each time, so the program hands it the whole pile of notes so far on every turn. That is also why long conversations cost more, and it leads straight into our context and memory topic.

Quick check, in your own words: if the runner never came back with a note, what would the desk person be able to tell the student?

I can turn this into a short lesson with a makerspace example when you're ready.
